The ROG Xbox Ally X20 makes for a fantastic upgrade over last year's vanilla X predecessor, but its higher price tag keeps it from getting any closer to portable perfection. Additions like its vibrant new OLED 1080P 120Hz display and controls that feel far more like an official console controller help justify its MSRP, but it's still going to be out of reach for plenty of players who deserve a solid portable PC experience.

Elevated controls that feel like a real Xbox controller

Same great performance from Ryzen Z2 Extreme as before

Slight enhancements to ergonomics via rubber grips and subtle changes

Xbox Big Screen Experience helps dilute pain of Windows 11

$1,300 is arguably too much for any handheld

No real performance improvements over last year's model

Why you can trust GamesRadar+ Our experts review games, movies and tech over countless hours, so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about our reviews policy.

Some say second time’s the charm; I tend to think third time’s lucky, but the ROG Xbox Ally X20 technically isn’t really a redo of Microsoft’s handheld gaming PC. Yes, it switches out the old 1080p 120Hz IPS display with the OLED panel it should have had in the first place and adds fancy new TMR sticks, but the upgrades feel geared toward a select few who’re actively willing to spend over $1,000 on a portable in 2026.

That is to say that while adding an OLED display to last year’s ROG Xbox Ally X absolutely elevates the visual experience and thoroughly pleased my peepers during testing, the X20’s price tag holds it back. If money were not an object, I’d automatically give the revamp its predecessor’s seat at the best gaming handheld table, but alas, paying $1,299.99 / £1,399.99 for the newbie comes down to your feelings about enhanced brightness and vibrancy.

Yes, this is the same “sweating button guy” meme situation sparked by the Steam Deck OLED back in 2024, so I’m not saying making a shiny new ROG Xbox X20 was a bad idea. In fact, throughout my time testing this new Ryzen Z2 Extreme contender, I’ve fallen even harder for its chonky controller grips and even its less-than-perfect console-inspired Xbox Big Screen Experience. The main issue is that, unlike when Valve popped a new panel on its portable, Asus and Microsoft have ramped up the price by $300.

I have a terrible relationship with time. I struggle with the passage of time and how quickly a calendar year loops back around. You could even call it a phobia, so upon grabbing onto the ROG Xbox Ally X20 for the first time, I was immediately hit with an eerie wave of Déjà vu that made me realize that the “OG” ROG Xbox Ally X was now 12 months old. However, rather than feeling like I’d blinked through into the future, I instead felt like I was back, taking a look at Microsoft’s portable for the first time.

I’m not for one second saying Asus should have overhauled its design language for the Xbox Ally X20. In fact, I’m thrilled that the handheld is hanging onto all of its evolved ergonomics, like its controller-inspired back grips, asymmetrical thumbstick layout, and visual cues that are closer to the PlayStation Portal than its portable PC kin.

At the same time, some players will be asking “what’s changed” with the ROG Xbox Ally X20, and while it does sport a rather dashing smoked transparent shell and gold accents, you’d be forgiven for thinking it’s just a new colorway. It technically is, but when you’re paying $300 more than the last time, and technically more again compared to the OG Asus ROG Ally, most players will want it to scream, “I am worth the hike.”

Let’s just say that on the aesthetics front, I’m pretty baffled that Microsoft decided not to nostalgia-bait players with a transparent green shell and OG Xbox-inspired face buttons. I’d pretty much assumed something similar to the X25 controller was a given, and I do think that, on its own, doesn’t justify a hike; it would have helped it feel more like a celebratory “special edition” 25th anniversary release. Instead, the “X20” is actually in honor of Asus’ Republic of Gamers brand and its 20th anniversary, which is, uh, perhaps not in your calendar if you’re here for the console vibes.

Hardware nerds unite, sign up to our free tech newsletter for a weekly digest of the hottest new tech, the latest gadgets on the test bench, and much more from the team at GamesRadar+.

If we’re talking purple about looks and feel, and you’re deliberating between the ROG Xbox Ally X20 and its vanilla X sibling, here are my observations on the subtleties. In the hands, the X20 manages to feel slightly posher, largely thanks to rubberized back grips and an increase in heft (756g vs 715g). The gold accents only just dodge garish accusations, and while the retro console editor in me naturally digs translucent tech, the smoke show only gives a slight glimpse of its innards under the right lighting conditions.

With that increased weight, I did find myself balancing my elbows on things more with the X20 compared to the original. It’s not aggressively heavier, and the rubber grips did help provide enhanced stability overall, especially when holding on for my life in Star Wars Galactic Racer. But otherwise, you’re talking about two handhelds that feel nearly identical to clutch, and the reasons to splurge on the newbie aren’t shell-deep.

I’m not quite done covering how the ROG Xbox Ally X20 feels to use, as Asus and Microsoft have done far more with the buttons, triggers, and sticks than you’d perhaps expect. Effectively, the handheld now feels almost like an actual Xbox controller rather than drawing influence from a third-party pad like the Asus ROG Raikiri Pro. The result is something that absolutely translates to a portable console experience, and it’s perhaps what we should have got the first time around.

I’ll note that the face buttons and sticks are virtually the same as before, but the latter does swap out traditional parts for TMR (Tunnel Magnetoresistance) tech, resulting in an accuracy boost and natural immunity to stick drift. The A,B,X,Y buttons feature the same snappy membranes as before, and since I had zero complaints with them before, it feels right that they made it to this second revision.

The real showstopper lies with the X20’s D-pad, triggers, and bumpers, as those now magically feel just like an Xbox Wireless Controller. The concave D-pad and its clicky dome contacts have finally usurped Asus's old design, meaning you’re getting all the tactile goodness the console provides to side-scroller lovers and fighting game enthusiasts alike. Even if you’re not into genres that explicitly leverage it, the added tactility and accuracy make all the difference when used as a toggle, with, again, Galactic Racer really shining when flicking speeder switches at the start of each race.

Xbox controllers also provide a very distinct set of triggers with dampening qualities, and while it’s included to dial back plasticky clunks, it also contributes to a very specific feel. The Xbox Ally X did attempt to emulate this, and I figured it had gotten pretty close to emulating the results. That was until I started playing on the X20 and swiftly realized there was room for improvement, as my brain instantly registered each trigger press as being just like my Robot White pad.

There’s admittedly not that much in the feel of the X20 controls vs. the X, but there’s enough to matter. Everything from the bounce of those triggers to the new-age Xbox D-pad helps reinforce the brand’s presence with this portable, and that’s really important when you’re clearly trying to target console players with dreams of playing their libraries on the go.

Look, it shouldn’t really be a surprise that the ROG Xbox Ally X20’s main selling point is the OLED screen, especially given that the accompanying specs haven’t changed. For what it’s worth, the switch-out makes for a tremendous visual experience that is geared to take on the Steam Deck OLED and win thanks to its 1080p 120Hz capabilities and higher brightness.

There are objective metrics that help spell out the OLED benefits on paper, like the fact you’re getting a larger 1080p 120Hz 7.4-inch panel that provides 297 pixels per inch with 1,400 nits HDR brightness (600 nits SDR), and FreeSync Premium Pro tricks. That’s enough to spell out where at least part of the extra $300 for this model is going, but I really want to capture the essence of what my eyeballs have enjoyed comparatively through testing.

I’ve spent enough time with IPS displays to know they just can’t keep up with OLED, and I’ve consistently felt underwhelmed with the ROG Xbox Ally X’s visuals compared to the Steam Deck OLED. Upon grabbing hold of the X20 for the first time, I sat upright on my bed in a dimly lit room in the exact same position I’d normally use its portable predecessor. If you want an embarrassing visual, picture me with my knees up, holding onto the pricey handheld like a steering wheel with my face far too close to the screen.

As far as my senses were concerned, I was clutching a familiar portable. Little did I know that booting up Star Wars Galactic Racer would immediately signal that I wasn’t in IPS Kansas anymore, as seeing that Fuse logo ignite in sparks of yellow on what looked like an off display completely set my expectations for the visual experience ahead.

The peak brightness of the X20 alone is a fantastic achievement, as it pierces daylight and outshines even south-facing windows in my house. Glare has the potential to be an issue since we’re talking about a glossy screen, but I found that the elevated brightness, and the fact that you will block any direct light hitting the screen most of the time during play with your own presence, means it’s virtually negligible.

I’ve argued on more than one occasion that vibrancy is often worth prioritising over other panel specs. Yes, playing games at 120Hz is lovely, and as I’ll get to, 1080p finally feels relevant in the portable realm thanks to chips like the Ryzen Z2 Extreme. But, I must admit that specs weren’t really on my mind while enjoying playing the MediEvil recomp over the spooky season, as the OLED screen fully pulled its weight in making the high-contrast PlayStation textures pop against the era-specific murky black short draw distances. Simply put, everything will look outstanding on this display, whether that means embracing HDR in Cyberpunk 2077 or messing with old PS1 romps.

Again, the X20 isn’t a sequel, and that means you’re not getting a generational revamp in terms of chip specs. On the AMD side of things, the Ryzen Z2 Extreme is as good as it gets for reasonable handhelds, and if you’re looking for a greater punch, you’ll either have to go for absurdly priced contenders by the likes of GPD WIN with a Ryzen AI MAX+ 395, or give Intel’s Arc G3 a try.

The real question you have to ask is whether you’re fine with paying $300 more to stick with virtually the same performance. It’s something I’ve been deliberating on while having an absolute blast playing games on the X20 at comparably lofty frame rates to the Steam Deck, and RAMageddon makes pointing price-point blame a little difficult. Still, there’s no getting around the fact that the same frame rate results for more money is a bad pitch, and it feels like this model exists to be an OLED fan crowd-pleaser.

Benchmarking the same hardware 12 months later can normally lead to some funky results. It’s something that used to worry me in my early days as a hardware reviewer, as it’d gaslight me into thinking I’d messed up my original test run. In reality, it’s usually due to performance nuances between Windows updates, game patches, and various other factors that can hinder or help boost fps, so keep that in mind when looking at the ROG Xbox Ally X vs. X20.

For science, I’m running benchmarks on the Xbox Ally X20 anyway, as they can serve as updated Ryzen Z2 Extreme results. Spoiler: there are no real surprises in these stats, and driver updates seemingly haven’t given the AMD chipset any newfound muscle. If anything, I seem to have lost a few inconsequential frames, but that’s tied to the pain of gaming on Windows overall.

Kicking things off just like before with Cyberpunk 2077, and we’re working with a 52fps average at 1080p with everything cranked down low. That’s with no upscaling assistance, but it paints a performance picture without using tools like AMD FSR. I did manage to hit 54fps last time on the Xbox Ally X, so the X20 is hitting the same sub-60fps spot as before.

That minor drop in comparative performance stands out a bit more in Total War: Warhammer 3, as for whatever reason, I lost around four frames compared to last time. I still hit 60fps in the RTS romp, even if only just, but it feels like something is happening under the Windows layers that’s preventing things from inching ahead compared to last time.

Weirdly, the trend continues with Shadow of the Tomb Raider, as I ended up with the same gap as with Cyberpunk 2077. It’s still within what I’d call a “margin of Windows fomfoolery”, as we’re talking 62fps vs 64 with the OG Xbox Ally X. I wouldn’t lose sleep over that difference, and chances are that it’s more just whatever the operating system is up to right now plus various other driver factors, but it draws a line under whether you’ll get higher performance via the OLED model.

Since I’ve been spending so much time tearing up the track in a speeder, it feels only right to include Star Wars Galactic Racer in my benchmarking run this time around. If for no other reason, I wanted to include an example of a game that will run exceptionally well while still looking the part on “lower-end” hardware compared to your PC or home console. Considering the sci-fi death race just landed, I’m actually pretty staggered by the portable experience provided, and I’ll be using it as a test title going forward.

I really wouldn’t recommend dialling everything down to low at 1080p for Star Wars Galactic Racer, but if you’re not fussed about gnarly graphics, you’ll be treated to an 115fps average. At least, that’s the figure I got on Jakku during testing, but I opted to spend my leisure time playing with medium settings and AMD’s FSR bells and whistles enabled. That ended up producing visuals at a 70fps average that really looked on par with a console on a small screen, and even some of the funky effects of Frame Interpolation were easy to look past thanks to the elevated vibrancy and that 120Hz refresh rate.

Last year, the ROG Xbox Ally X arrived alongside Microsoft’s answer to SteamOS: Xbox Big Screen Experience. It’s essentially an overlay for Windows 11, meant to ditch the notion that you’re using a bloated operating system primarily for desktop machines. I figured that over the span of twelve months, the Xbox-themed HUD would have evolved into something befitting of a next-gen console like Project Helix, but, uh, it feels like very little has changed.

Yes, micro upgrades have been pushed out, as Xbox Big Screen Experience now has a more fleshed-out Gamebar, optimized performance, and expanded compatibility with more portables. From a user perspective, though, all the irritating little bugs and quirks remain from last year, and in the instances where I did have a better time navigating the UI, it felt like I’d simply gotten more familiar with the overlay.

Here’s the thing: I quite like the Xbox Big Screen Experience. At least, I find it preferable to going anywhere near Windows 11’s desktop. Jumping into games across almost every storefront is faster thanks to the carousel tab system, and getting a full view of your library in one place is a natural boon. Just don’t expect the Epic Games Store to remotely play nice on any of these portables, especially now that vibe coding has entered the scene (heads up: if you can’t access your library in Xbox Mode, adjust your desktop scaling).

I could write a whole article on Xbox Mode and all of its handheld hangups, including its tendency not to auto-switch to freshly opened applications, launch two instances of games like Cyberpunk 2077, and randomly decide to ignore the built-in controls. I might even still delve into all of that separately if I can, but my main takeaway is that it’s better than vanilla Windows 11. So long as you can brace yourself for a little bit of jank, you’ll have a cromulent console-inspired experience in your hands.

I’m hesitant to say the handheld PC scene hasn’t worked to resolve its glaring battery life issues. Asus specifically has been cramming chonkier 80Whr cells into its portables since before its Xbox partnership, and the new X20 model carries that baton with expected playtimes of around 3-4 hours in demanding romps.

The age-old catch of having to dial back screen brightness and wattage remains, though. Left to my own devices, I found that the X20 would putter out at around the two-hour mark, notably in games like Star Wars: Galactic Racer using 30W Turbo Mode. That’s longer than you’ll get out of some portables out there, particularly those that use traditional 40-50Wh cells while still pushing for higher wattages, but it’ll still result in you reaching for a high-wattage charger shortly into sessions.

There are instances where you’ll absolutely get Switch 2 runtimes out of the Xbox Ally X20. For instance, I was able to get around 5 hours into my MediEvil Recomp playthrough before seeking a power source, which is a testament to efficiency. The Z2 Extreme itself also provides some headroom for messing around with settings and wattage to hit an experience that won’t tank your longevity, even if that does mean sacrificing 60fps in some scenarios.

I can’t hide my distaste for spending over $1,000 on any handheld gaming PC, given that the scene kickstarted with far cheaper contenders just a few years ago. It’s that price tag that ultimately prevents the ROG Xbox Ally X20 from soaring past its ever-so-slightly more affordable LCD sibling. However, its fabulous OLED panel and defined controls help the premium portable reach similar heights in my eyes, with the upgrades just about justifying the hikes for players who appreciate fancy perks.

That is to say that the ROG Xbox Ally X20 is one of the best gaming handhelds money can buy, but that doesn’t mean you should do just that. For some, this powerhouse will be a worthwhile investment that should be cheaper, but will deliver a notable on-the-go PC gaming experience in 2026. For others, it’s another princely portable that doesn’t offer enough of a revolutionary experience over older alternatives to be a viable option.

My regulars will be tired of reading this, but the gaming hardware scene, and I guess the world at large, is having a moment. Everything is inflated, costing more than it should and suffering through needlessly convoluted manufacturing circumstances that threaten the existence of consumer tech as a whole. In a way, the ROG Xbox Ally X20 is just another victim of RAMageddon, and that means while it’s objectively great, there are plenty of subjective reasons why you shouldn’t give in to paying more for it.

Over the course of a month, I used the ROG Xbox Ally X20 to benchmark a selection of test games while playing recent releases like Star Wars Galactic Racer in my spare time. Throughout testing, I assessed the portable's perceived and measurable performance while noting the overarching qualitative experience and physical feel of the device. In addition to playing contemporary games, I also made time to test projects like the MediEvil Recomp to get a feel for the device's low-end abilities side by side with its handling of big-budget releases using its Ryzen Z2 Extreme chipset.

For more information on how we test gaming handhelds and other portable gadgets, swing by our full GamesRadar+ hardware policy for a deep dive.

In the past, they have covered everything from retro gaming history to the latest gaming news, in-depth features, and tech advice for publications like TechRadar, The Daily Star, the BBC, PCGamesN, and Den of Geek. In their spare time, they pour hours into fixing old consoles, modding Game Boys, exploring ways to get the most out of the Steam Deck, and blasting old CRT TV visuals into their eye sockets.

#3682. Nvidia's latest graphics card driver appears to be unnecessarily writing to PC SSDs, something that's dumb, annoying and definitely warrants reverting

Ooh, an Nvidia-related story that isn't about their now former CEO allegedly getting amorous with someone. I wonder what it's abou-oh. Oh no. It looks like Nvidia's latest GeForce driver, 621.24, is needlessly writing vast amounts of data to PC SSDs.

As noted by PC Gamer, reports of driver 621.24 writing more than it should to SSDs have popped up across various forums and Reddit.

Some instances of the bug, which doesn't appear to be affecting everyone, have the driver writing up to 30GB every hour. For context, it'd take a bugged driver writing that much thousands of hours to break a gaming SSD with a typical endurance rating in the hundreds of terabytes. However, that doesn't mean this is anything less than a pretty bad bug. As such, reverting to the previous driver, 621.01, is a good idea if you're on 621.24 and suspect it of writing chunks of gigabytes to your SSD.

In order to check if that's going on, open task manager, head to the 'details' tab, right click on the column header, click 'select columns', select 'I/O write bytes' from the menu of check boxes that brings up, then look for 'NVDisplay.Container.exe'. The number next that exe is in bytes, so you'll need to do a bit of maths to work out if it's writing mere MB or globs of GB.

Bizarrely, the affected 621.24 driver still hasn't been pulled by Nvidia as of writing, meaning it can still be downloaded by people who might not be aware of any issues and think 'ooh, haven't checked I'm on the latest driver in a while.' The driver was released on November 12th, so it's not a brand new arrival that the company just haven't had a chance to look into yet.

Here's hoping that it is fixed or replaced ASAP, if it hasn't been by the time you read this. AMD look to have dealt with a similar issue recently, and I'd like to think driver updates across all cards aren't going to be some form of permanent Russian roulette going forwards.

Unreal Engine 6 will not launch with the engine's long-standard Blueprints scripting system. The news came in a Friday, November 19 post on the Unreal Engine website, written by Epic Games executive vice president of development, Marcus Wassmer. Here's Wassmer's top-level summary from the post:

"UE6, including UE6 Early Access, won’t include Blueprints or the Actor Gameplay Framework. Gameplay will be built in Verse and on the new Scene Graph framework.

"In June, we said Blueprints and Actors would coexist in UE6 Early Access and 6.0, so UE5 projects could upgrade incrementally while the new Scene Graph framework matures. However, with recent advances in AI capability, we expect AI to massively help with converting UE5 projects to UE6, if not make that process fully automatic. That also means we can deliver UE6 on time (or sooner!) while meeting its design goals: a new data model, a Verse-first architecture, modularity, and AI operability."

Blueprints have not (and it appears, will not) be deprecated in Unreal Engine 5, and the company maintains that projects will still be easy to convert from UE5 to UE6. Wassmer cited a declining cost in AI task completion as one reason for this belief, as well as the team's ongoing, but apparently successful conversion of Fortnite's Blueprint library to UE6's Verse programming language through an AI-assisted process.

Blueprints are a widely-used feature of Unreal. Former Valve developer Chet Faliszek, an AI skeptic, has put out a vlog on the subject. Essentially, Faliszek argues that Blueprints (and features like them in other game engines) represent a middle ground between artistic and technical work, an introduction and skill builder for less technically-minded developers. Without them, such developers seemingly have to either learn Verse code, or integrate LLM prompting into their workflows.

"We made a new skill in the middle there, between normal and expert," Faliszek said of intermediate tools like Blueprints. "To lose that determinism from game design, and instead have to prompt AI⁠—or write your own Verse … It's losing those tools that made all those designers and all those artists so powerful, to be able to do really powerful things and have access to really deep-down things, but in a safe way that the engineers can decide what that meant to them."

A dark horse game of the year candidate, the first-person RPG Queen's Domain, was made with Unreal Engine. I recently spoke to co-developer Eric Berger, who specialized in art and design alongside the more technically-focused Bradley Boothe, a relationship that rhymes with the ones Faliszek outlined in his video.

I spoke to Berger before seeing Epic's latest press release, but Berger already indicated that Unreal's AI pivot is prompting Freshly Baked Games to switch engines for its next project. I followed up with Berger about this Blueprint news, and the developer said that Blueprints were a major part of the workflow on Queen's Domain.

I'm a layman in game development, but I think Wassmer's post elides that there is a large qualitative difference between doing any work via LLM prompt versus the old-fashioned way⁠—I don't like or want to use these tools, myself, and I don't think that's an unpopular stance. Commenter ZILtoid1991 on Faliszek's video compared the move to Apple removing headphone jacks on the iPhone, a comparison I find fruitful.

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

It was hugely unpopular at the time, and is still derided by enthusiasts, but it also worked. Other manufacturers copied Apple, and everybody has bluetooth headphones now⁠—or Apple's own, proprietary Air Pods. But Apple had far less success trying something similar with its laptops: The lack of ports on late 2010s Macbooks proved disastrous, and Apple has since reintroduced more (and a wider variety of) ports on newer models of the popular line. I certainly have my own anti-AI, pro-headphone jack preferences, but we'll have to see how this plays out with the Unreal Engine.

#3680. Warren Spector lambasts GTA 6's "billion dollar" development - 'I just hope it's is the last of its kind even if it's the best we have to offer'

"A billion dollars pays for a lot of games and a lot of salaries."

As GTA 6 finally arrives, increasingly outspoken games industry legend Warren Spector - known for seminal immersive sims including Deus Ex - has offered both praise for the game's achievements and lambasted its "billion dollar" development model, writing, "I just hope GTA 6 is the last of its kind even if it’s the best we have to offer".

Spector announced his retirement from games development in August following struggles at his OtherSide Entertainment studio, and has been vocal about the state of the games industry in the months since, notably saying anyone at EA responsible for the "travesty" of BioWare's closure should be "ashamed". And now Spector has taken on GTA 6.

"First, congratulations to everyone who worked on GTA 6. It looks like it will be a high point of sorts for our medium and our business," he wrote in a post on LinkedIn. "However… its billion dollar development cost and an undoubtedly crazy marketing budget don't represent a business model anyone else can or probably should emulate.

"That's especially true," Spector continued, "when thousands of developers are out of work. A billion dollars pays for a lot of games and a lot of salaries. Personally I'd rather have hundreds of games and full employment than one game no matter how amazing it is."

The "sure success" of GTA 6 proves a point he's made "for years", he said: "That no game that matters ships on time and/or on budget". Highlighting GTA 6's year-long delay and reported billion dollar budget, Spector suggested, "Give a game the time and money to prove its potential (key word, potential) and you have a chance of making something great. Underfund a game or force it out the door before it's ready [is] guaranteed failure no matter how much potential it has.

"So, again, congratulations," Spector concluded. "Ambition and innovation are necessary for the medium to reach its potential. I just hope GTA 6 is the last of its kind even if it's the best we have to offer."

Despite Spector's concerns, GTA 6's arrival is, as expected, already causing shockwaves across the industry. It has broken pre-order records for Xbox and PlayStation stores, smashed the all-time livestream viewer record, and apparently briefly broke Reddit too. And is its success deserved? Arion Kurtaj, the now 21-year-old hacker behind the massive GTA 6 leak of 2022, has been released from prison, as a judge warns that he shouldn't try this kind of hack again.

Kurtaj was 16 years old when his hacks against Rockstar began alongside other members of hacking group Lapsus$. Following the release of at least 90 videos featuring early GTA 6 gameplay, Kurtaj was deemed psychiatrically unfit for trial and was eventually sentenced to a lifetime stay in a secure hospital because of his severe autism. Rockstar said that the hack had cost it $5 million.

But Kurtaj's status changed in January, when he was transferred to a standard prison ahead of a planned retrial. Last week, he pleaded guilty to hacks against Rockstar and others.

Kurtaj has been given a seven-year sentence and released on the same day, as the BBC reports. He had already served the majority of that sentence during his time in the secure hospital and prison. The judge, Mr. Justice Turner, told Kurtaj "you are a very talented young man," but offered a warning: "Don't let this happen again."

The hacker has been released on license which, for my fellow Americans, is essentially a form of parole. He's been given a five-year Serious Crime Prevention Order restricting him from using online services including Telegram and Discord.

Of course, this isn't the only hacking incident Rockstar is dealing with. Ahead of launch, a hacking group or individual known as Cyberleek released numerous gameplay videos from a seemingly near-final build of GTA 6. Now, Cyberleek has released an Xbox build of the game which modders are working to turn into a full-blown PC port. At this point, it's possible that an unofficial GTA 6 PC port could land before Rockstar can deliver an official version.

GTA 6 update gives players losing progress to crashes a lifeline – and it looks like the first-person and 60fps glitches are safe for now

#3676. Does GTA 6 have an 'easy mode'? Not officially, but there are two very important settings you can change to make the game less difficult

By now, you've probably heard that you cannot use cheats in GTA 6 until you complete the main story. Not only that, but enabling cheat codes also locks story progression and deactivates the ability to save. Basically, you can use cheats to have a quick crime spree and blow off some steam, then it's back to normalcy. Understandably, some gamers are a little put out with this change.

But, for anyone looking to have a slightly easier time with GTA 6 than the dev's intended experience, I come with good news: you can make the game a little bit easier by toggling two options in the game's Settings menu. If you open Settings, and then navigate to Gameplay, you'll find 'Accessible Combat' and 'Reduced Vehicle Damage' toggles. You can activate both to make GTA 6's more difficult elements a little bit easier to work through.

'Accessible Combat' decreases enemy health and makes them deal less damage to your character — the kind of rebalancing that you'd expect from a traditional difficulty slider. 'Reduced Vehicle Damage', as you'd expect, lowers the damage taken by your vehicle and allows your ride to endure more punishment. This applies to gunfire, environmental threats, and impact damage.

Toggle these settings comes with a warning from Rockstar, though. A prompt notes that enabling these modifiers will "significantly change the balance and experience of the gameplay". I've been playing around with these settings and whilst they are not a foolproof 'God Mode' by any means, you can absolutely see a difference in the game when they're enabled: Jason and Lucia take a lot more punishment from melee damage and gunshots, and I had to really try to get Jason's old banged up pickup into even the 'slightly smoking' bracket of disrepair. Your mileage may vary, but these settings, from what I can tell so far, certainly do make the game easier.

Given that cheats disable trophies and progression, these settings might be something to keep in mind if you're trying to find a smoother path through the main story of GTA 6. It's a credit to Rockstar's accessibility teams that these have been included at all - alongside the 23 other gameplay accessibility options, the 12 display options, the 70 UI options, the 24 camera options, and the 14 audio options.

"We create inclusive, intuitive, and immersive experiences for every player," noted Rockstar's associate UI director, Sam Grosset, in materials provided to Eurogamer ahead of the game's launch. "Accessibility is considered from the outset, and designing for diverse needs enables us to create better games for everyone. We wanted every player in GTA 6 to have options to play the game how they like. Whether it's selecting a larger font size, opting for a more minimal screen experience, or making a controls tweak to sprinting... the choices are open to all."

We also learned yesterday that Rockstar has made GTA 6 missions "harder to fail" by making them more open-ended, and giving players more ways to figure out how to do things in their own way.

If you need a hand with any of the myriad things GTA 6 asks you to do, you can read Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough as well as a breakdown of Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

#3675. Darkest Dungeon 2's next bit of DLC is a short run, combat focused gauntlet where you must do everything in your power to please the audience

The original Darkest Dungeon may have gotten some new DLC earlier this year, but that doesn't mean that Red Hook Studios are abandoning their sequel. No, in fact the next bit of DLC for Darkest Dungeon 2 was teased only a couple of weeks ago, with a new trailer shared today actually showing off what it's all about.

It's called The Butcher's Asylum, as pleasant a name as any other, and it's a "stand alone gladiatorial arena game mode," that's due for release sometime in 2027. "The long-silent bells of the remote Asylum ring once more - souring the valley below with discordant and unsettling vibrations," the DLC's Steam page describes. "Garish heraldry, hastily stitched by unskilled hands, festoons the hilltop. Deep within the crumbling masonry of the Asylum, frenzied inmates compete in merciless bloodsport with monsters corralled the kingdom over. And to the victors of these debauched contests, the Butcher’s favour: a cure for their madness."

This DLC isn't veering too far away from its roguelite origins, as it is still run-based, just on the shorter side and focusing more on the combat system. On your runs you'll need to prepare for the fights ahead, come across "insane enemy combinations never before possible," and spin a fun wheel which nets you prizes like new battle modifiers, charms and jinxes. There's also a new crowd meter, "a unique feature to the Asylum, can grant powerful effects to your team if you cater to the Crowd's demands. Failing to do so will only earn their scorn which raises the stakes and puts your success in jeopardy!"

The Butcher's Asylum also introduces a new playable character, The Ringmaster. You pick her up by winning bouts in the arena, and then you can recruit her in any game mode. She also serves as the narrator for the DLC, likely because of the passing of the main game's narrator Wayne June; Red Hook made clear earlier this year that they would never use generative AI to recreate June's voice, so I'm glad to see they haven't backstracked here.

A choice (or two!) can lead to drastically different endings.

Please note, this guide contains massive spoilers for some of the endings of Grand Theft Auto 6. If you don't want to know what happens, please stop reading!

There are multiple endings to GTA 6, and not all the endings take place in the same location. One of the potential final scenes during the GTA 6 story mission, The End of the Road, takes place on a bridge in the Leonida Keys.

After discovering the cops are onto them, Jason and Lucia drive away from Cal's house and head to Brian's marina to find an airplane. The police quickly trap them on a bridge with a roadblock ahead and multiple cars behind them. Lucia wants to keep going but Jason thinks it's all over for them. The player is then given a choice, "Swim for it" or "No Surrender."

AGAIN, MASSIVE SPOILERS BELOW! STOP NOW IF YOU DON'T WANT TO KNOW THE ENDINGS!

Jason and Lucia decide Tomas is better off without them in his life. They drive through the roadblock, shooting at the cops. They're both shot to death and we see them dead in the front seat of the car, still holding hands. During the end credits, we see Tomas living happily with Lucia's aunt and her husband and children.

Jason and Lucia decide to jump off the bridge and swim to freedom.

However, a second choice appears once you've chosen 'Swim for it.' As Jason gets out of the car, a prompt for Lucia to 'Exit' the car appears. You can choose for Lucia to follow through with the plan by pressing the button, or change your mind and let the prompt expire.

A: 'Swim for it' and 'Exit': The couple will get out of the car together and walk to the edge of the bridge. Lucia jumps but Jason does not, letting himself get arrested by the cops. During the credits, Lucia signs the deal which keeps her free and sends Jason to prison. We see her bring Tomas to visit him, so Jason finally meets his son, though it's through glass.

B: 'Swim for it' and don't 'Exit': If you choose to swim for it but don't choose the 'Exit' prompt, Jason will get out of the car but Lucia will remain in the car. The police will open fire and kill them both. As with the No Surrender option, we see Tomas living with Lucia's aunt's family.

C: 'Swim for it' and 'Exit' (with $2 million in Buck Me savings): If you delayed the Protective Custody mission of GTA 6 until you had deposited $2 million in savings, the Swim for it and Exit choices will show the same results, but during the credits, Lucia uses the money to get Jason released from prison. Lucia picks him up at prison, and Jason meets Tomas and holds his hand.

Note: These are not the only endings to GTA 6. I've seen several more endings that do not take place on the bridge at all and don't involve these particular choices.

I have been inundated with GTA 6-related advertising over the last few weeks. Every company on the planet has been in my inbox with some kind of press release tying their product to this massive new release - just this morning I was emailed by a bedding company about all the hours of sleep people must have missed out on in order to pull all-nighters in Leonida. But perhaps the most interesting tie-in comes from Pavel Durov, founder and CEO of messaging service Telegram.

Telegram, if you're not aware, is a messaging platform that is best known for its security, driven by end-to-end encryption and self-destructing messages that make it pretty good for keeping information secret. This makes it pretty popular with, say, investigative journalists, but has also given Telegram a bit of a reputation as something that's also a bit handy if you're a career criminal looking to keep people off your trail. Of course, that particular reputation is not something the company's founder and CEO would be keen to lean into. Or so you might think...

Late last night, Durov tweeted that "the least realistic thing about GTA 6 is that Jason and Lucia run a whole criminal operation without a single Telegram group." Now, I get it. I get the desire to seem like you're part of the zeitgeist, like you're linked to this major new cultural touchstone, and to organically tie your product into that conversation. What I don't entirely get is the impulse to say the quiet part out loud.

The least realistic thing about GTA VI is that Jason and Lucia run a whole criminal operation without a single Telegram group.November 22, 2026

If I know that Telegram is probably pretty useful if you want to keep your illicit dealings secret, Durov must definitely know that. However, Durov also has a product to sell and (presumably) a reputation to uphold as a fine, upstanding citizen who definitely isn't making criminals' lives easier. Put aside for now the fact that GTA 6 has a dedicated 'steal this car' app, and I might avoid making the link between the game and my app so explicitly about crime. Especially given that GTA makes up its own parody software companies to ape those in the real world, and you'd think Durov might have decided to sit this one out.

#3671. "Everyone agrees it's more fun this way": Toby Fox won't tell his team how Deltarune ends until they've built enough of it

"Just when the story reached a critical moment, I stopped reading…"

Toby Fox is a purposefully mysterious person. It was probably a wise choice on his part, obfuscating his current appearance with everyone's favourite annoying dog, essentially never speaking aloud in livestreams and instead using a text-to-speech bot, and posting only when there's notable enough Deltarune updates of if it would be very funny. But as it turns out, that sense of mystery extends to the team that's making Deltarune too, as Fox won't tell his devs how the game ends until they've built enough of it.

Earlier this week, the fall edition of the Deltarune newsletter went out, offering a brief update on the game's next and sixth chapter. That one's apparently now a "structurally complete draft that can be played from the beginning to the end," but that doesn't mean it's quite ready for release, as "some important scenes and details are still undercooked in their presentation." I'd expect a 2027 release for this chapter, which is going to be a shorter one too.

But in typical tricky Tony fashion, there's an update for chapter seven where he makes it sound like no one but him knows how the whole game is going to end. "Well, we've only just started…," he explains of the progress. "I read out the events and dialogue of Chapter 7 to the team. However, just when the story reached a critical moment, I stopped reading… I told my team they need to complete more of the game before I tell them what happens. Everyone agrees it's more fun this way."

I'm glad they all think it's fun, the wait for me personally certainly ain't. I do wonder if this speaks to a certain anxiety over how the game will shape up. Following the release of chapter five I was subjected to all manner of theories about what's to come by my partner gorging on YouTube videos from folks who mostly just seem quite excited about it all, even if a lot of them sound wrong. So I imagine there must be a little bit of weight to all of those varying expectations.

Fox did note in the newsletter that "unlike every other Chapter, I actually feel like I know what I'm doing this time, so I have a lot of confidence...!" so perhaps I'm speaking a load of hogwash! That said, I'm furious that a character called Apple Girlington didn't make it into chapter five, so you can expect to hear from my lawyers, Mr. Fox.

Over the last couple of weeks, some Nvidia users noticed their SSDs were taking a hammering, reporting their driver's log file was being overwritten constantly, sometimes to the tune of 30 GB every hour. Which obviously isn't great for the lifespan of the valuable SSD you've got it installed on.

Given the problem was caused by recent driver updates, rolling back to version 621.01 was the best solution until Nvidia could do something about it. Which they did, releasing a hotfix as version 621.35. It's not available in the GeForce app yet, but you can download it directly from Nvidia's site. Not that you should.

As users on the Nvidia subreddit are reporting, the problem persists. While the hotfix reduces the peak write rate and prevents it for a short while after reboot, it eventually creeps back in. One user reported that overnight the log file was still being rewritten by approximately 4.5 GB every hour.

So yeah, the best solution remains to roll back to version 621.01 and, as always with Nvidia drivers, to hold off on updating to the latest driver until it's been confirmed safe. If this ongoing saga sounds familiar, it's because the same thing happened to AMD's GPU drivers earlier this month. Maybe vibecoding driver updates and then vibecoding fixes for their inevitable bugs isn't the best way of doing things.

#3668. Eldritch Empathy is a Papers Please-esque roguelite about diagnosing cosmic horror creatures and trying not to lose your marbles as you do

Oh I do love an eldritch horror creature, I do, especially one that at first glance may only be slightly different from what I'm used to seeing. Eldritch Empathy, then, seems like a grand ole game to satisfy my wanton need to experience such things. It's a puzzle roguelite that isn't exactly a Papers Please-like but certainly feels reminiscent of one, where you have to "analyse corrupted creatures, purify their emotions and learn how to communicate with an eldritch being."

You kick things off by embodying Eike, a "young woman who has strange dreams and sightings of twisted creatures in the woodlands neighbouring the sleepy Swiss village she lives in." She decides to investigate these mysterious circumstances herself, where she comes upon these corrupted critters in the woods. You need to thoroughly inspect them, using a book to determine what is going on with them and what they need exactly; it's akin to checking the passport rulebook in Papers Please, hence the comparison.

After figuring out what's going on with these creatures, you then "use and transform symbols to create paths through the creatures' insides. You may use care and precision to navigate to the correct corrupted emotion you have identified from your investigation and purify it. You may also use your tools to cause harm. Whatever you choose, your actions will have consequences." Ominous! You can also plan your runs ahead of time, heading down paths that may offer you some boons here and there, like the option to restore a bit of sanity (it's one of those Lovecraftian kind of horror games, as loathe as I am that we still have to reference that guy).

Also be wary of the fact that actions you take out in the woods can affect your home and community. It's a roguelite with consequences! Mwahahha! Looks pretty neat overall, and has some tasty pixel art attached to it too. No release date just yet, but I'd assume it'll arrive no earlier than next year. You can wishlist it right here.

Former Dragon Age lead Mark Darrah says poor management from EA led to BioWare's was shutdown.

Mass Effect and Dragon Age maker BioWare was shut down by EA shortly after the publisher was acquired by a group of private investors. The studio – while beloved for its legendary RPGs across a 30-year history – had faced a ton of issues over its final few years with high-profile titles like Mass Effect: Andromeda, Anthem, and Dragon Age: The Veilguard failing to impress fans. Some pointed fingers at the studio itself for its demise.

Speaking to Pembridge (via PC Gamer) Darrah recalls an unnamed person's read on the situation: "EA doesn't shoot you, it puts a gun on the table and then comes in everyday and asks you if you'll shoot yourself."

He adds, "they just keep coming in over and over until eventually you just are like 'Ugh, fine. Just stop bugging me about it, I'll do it,'" in regards to EA's approach to BioWare.

"The reality is that EA can legitimately say 'we didn't make BioWare do this, they chose to do this,'" Darrah explains, "but if you dig underneath that statement the reality is that the options on the table were all terrible. We chose the least terrible of the options."

He points to BioWare's pivot to the Frostbite engine, Dragon Age 2's breakneck development cycle, and the whole situation with Anthem as things that were brought about by pressure from EA.

"They basically said [you] got to hit your financials. So what are you going to do?" Darrah adds, "Did they make us make Dragon Age 2? No. But they made us do something."

#3666. Over 2 million Xbox players in the UK and US reportedly used the 'New Zealand trick' to play GTA 6 early - that's more than a third of the country's population

We already knew there'd be a frantic clamour for GTA 6 this week, and we also knew plenty of players would be eyeing up Xbox's 'New Zealand trick' to get in on the action early. But it's now being reported that a whopping 2m UK and US players took advantage of the trick - which, for context, equals more than a third of New Zealand's actual population.

Here's a quick bit of background: Rockstar's regional release schedule meant GTA 6 launched at midnight on 19th November everywhere, local time. As such, New Zealand was the first country in the world to see the hugely anticipated game go live, thanks to timezones. And because Xbox players can make purchases on any regional store easily, simply by changing their console's country, understandably impatient sorts opted to become temporary virtual New Zealand residents in their droves (on PlayStation, the process requires a regional account and payment in local currency so is more finicky).

In fact, according to data analytics firm Ampere Analysis, the early demand was such that 1.5m Xbox users in the US and 600,000 UK Xbox players briefly went Kiwi for the occasion of GTA 6's launch. Other countries highlighted by Ampere include Canada, where 200,000 Xbox players took the New Zealand plunge, Brazil (200,000 players), and Mexico (100,000 players).

By contrast, just 100,000 PlayStation players in the US opted to dive in early, reflecting, as Ampere notes, "the ease of being able to switch country in the account settings on Xbox consoles." And here's all that info in graph form:

Amusingly, New Zealand's tourist board tipped a wink to the sudden influx of virtual 'visitors', telling them "We'd love to have you". It also cheekily offered a video of cheerful tourists admiring the country's resplendent natural beauty "Life," read the accompanying caption, "because we're getting GTA 6 first."

Some hours later and the rest of the world can now finally, officially join in the GTA 6 fun, and it's a game worth playing. Eurogamer's Chris Tapsell called it an open world of "awe, minute detail and impossible scale" in his five star GTA 6 review. And if you need some help getting through the game now it's here, you can check out Eurogamer's Grand Theft Auto 6 walkthrough as well as a breakdown of our Grand Theft Auto 6 cheats.

#3665. Public-access television is born anew in NIGHT EYE TV, a digital goggle box filled with art game curios

I am both a bit too young and a bit too very not American to have ever experienced public-access television, but it's something that's always fascinated me. For those too young to have even heard of it, or just not in the know, it essentially allowed anyone to broadcast their own shows through cable TV. A proto YouTube, if you will. It's obviously not what it was any more, given the advent of the internet, but in NIGHTEYE.TV, it may be making a digital, more interactive return.

NIGHTEYE.TV is a strange little place. I call it a place, it's a fake TV floating in a Unity default texture void, lending it a Backroomsian vibe, but even if there's not much there to ground yourself in, the goggle box is enticing all the same. It beckons you to turn it on, a series of buttons all linking to different "channels." What awaits you isn't television, however. Instead you'll find games, mostly of the weirdo, freako, sicko variety, quickly setting the tone.

🌕NIGHT EYE TV’s initial form is live!🌑 Check out the site and follow our Indiegogo campaign at www.nighteye.tv![image or embed]

In its current incarnation, it's mostly just a collection of clips of these various art games, with direct links to them hidden away in a menu, but a good collection it is. You'll find Nathalie Lawhead's Everything is Going to Be OK, Jeremy Couillard's more recent Soul Injector Commando, and Taylor McCue's He Fucked The Girl Out Of Me. Some clips are longer than others, acting as sort of segments of playthroughs, but it all feels like an exciting evolution of what public-access television was.

The ultimate goal is for it to be a curated platform where you can buy a rotating selection of games. Most of the sale goes back to the original artist, and 15% gets put into a community pool to be split amongst all of the contributors, with the last 15% going towards keeping everything running. As it stands, that's not quite ready yet. You can help make it happen, though, as right now an Indiegogo campaign is running to help it all get fully operational. Worth chucking a few quid I reckon!

As well as giving a spit-and-polish digital release to various Warhammer classics, antique D&D games, and the cult ellipsoid horror games in the Ecstatica series, SNEG has been bug-fixing a bunch of strategy games from years gone by and getting them up on Steam and GOG. The latest trio to appear on digital platforms are Theocracy, Soldiers at War, and Warlords 4: Heroes of Etheria.

Warlords 4 was the final turn-based game in the beloved series, with the RTS spin-off series Warlords Battlecry already two games deep by the time of its release in 2003. This updated version supports resolutions up to 4K, and incorporates community fixes and a community-made campaign. It's available on Steam and GOG.

Soldiers at War took the X-COM/UFO turn-based tactics formula—this was 1998, X-COM still had a hyphen—and applied it to World War II. You'd choose a squad of eight from your platoon of 32 each mission, fighting through a campaign that started in North Africa and ended in Germany, gaining experience along the way. SNEG's version supports 1280x720 widescreen resolution. It's available on Steam and GOG.

Theocracy narrowly beat Total War to the punch in March of 2000 with its mix of turn-based civilization management and real-time battles, tasking you with uniting Aztec tribes before the prophesied Spanish invasion. You're on the clock with 100 years to use diplomacy, trade, and warfare to bring together an empire that can stand the test of time. The updated version still has a resolution of 800x600, but uses FSR 1 to scale up for modern displays. You'll be shocked to learn, it's also available on Steam and GOG.

All three games are designed to be easy to run on modern Windows systems, and have cloud saves and achievements. I'm tempted by Warlords 4, which I didn't play at the time because I'd moved over to the real-time Battlecry games by then. But I've still got fond memories of Warlords 2 Deluxe, which had 60 different worlds so if you were tired of raising griffon armies in its generic fantasy land you could conquer something oddball like Dante's Inferno instead. Or even make your own, right down to pixel-crafting the unit art. Good times.

#3663. 8 Amazing Indie Games We Think You Should Go Play

Indie GamesQueen's DomainSonic Pico ParkTanuki: Pon's SummerWell Dweller

I’m seeing reports that some folks have already blazed through GTA 6‘s story, finishing the game roughly 48-ish hours (depending on your time zone) after its release. And of course, there are those gamers who don’t plan on playing the game at all, untouched by the powerfully seductive force of GTA 6 FOMO. Whatever your reason for having a free gaming calendar right now, I’ve come bearing gifts with which you can fill it. I’ve sampled my Kotaku colleagues as well as conducted my own research to assemble a smattering of recently released indie games you can play right now.

Dig Dig Dino was originally released on the Playdate before coming to Steam this week. It’s from the developers of the well-liked western action game Arco, though this time they’ve gone for something much smaller, simpler, and cuter. In Dig Dig Dino you play as an paleontology intern tasked with using your shovel and a growing arsenal of tools to find dinosaur bones. You start with limited stamina, only able to dig so much in a day. But as you chew through layers of dirt and sedimentary rock, you pick up treasure that gets exchanged for cash with which you can buy more more stamina, upgrades for your tools, and new tools like a dog who will sniff out bones for you.

The game sounds almost too simplistic to be any kind of fun, but I found myself spending hours digging, hoping the next run would reveal the final piece to my saurian puzzle. There are different dig sites that require different tools and yield different treasures, but don’t expect to discover the kinds of finds that would excite the dearly departed Dr. Alan Grant. The dinos you discover in this game are weird, and though I’m only a few hours (and a few competed skeletons) in, I suspect there’s a greater mystery about the world to discover as you dig deeper.

Sonic Pico Park may have the blue blur in the name, but itâs developed by the small team at TECOPARK, which created the original Pico Park. The cooperative puzzler lends some Sonic the Hedgehog flair toÂ Pico Park‘s cooperative, ragebait puzzle platforming action. The game is a lot of chaotic fun in which up to eight players will yell at one another, then lock in to solve some difficult challenges. Maybe you’re a big fan of Dark Souls, Elden Ring, or even King’s Field. Maybe you’re craving that next Elder Scrolls. Or maybe you’re just not super interested in cars and guns and want something a bit more medieval. Friends, let’s pay a visit to Queen’s Domain, a gorgeous first-person RPG in classic-PlayStation style that combines a very clonky, retro-feeling combat and exploration system with much more smoothness to movement and menuing than the games that inspired it could ever muster. Queen’s Domain has you exploring a mysterious island full of magic and monsters in search of your father. You’re puny and weak when you start, enemies hit hard and sneak up on you, and for the most part the game tells you very little about how to proceed: you just have to experiment and pray. But that’s exactly what some people (like me) want, and the feeling when something finally clicks is exhilirating. #3662. Alt Video is a digital, faux Blockbuster video store that you can fill with movies from your Letterboxd watchlist and Plex server

And you can even watch those movies in-game

Since the beginning of the year, I have watched almost 150 films. I know this, because over the past few years, I've become one of those people… a Letterboxd user. Gasp! I know, I know, but I don't think I'm too insufferable about it. I'll only do a joke review in the hopes of like farming if I think it's genuinely funny! But many of these films were watched digitally, meaning I don't have a bunch of DVDs to admire on a shelf. So what am I to do? Well, I could check out Alt Video, a not quite job simulator where you can use your Letterboxd account or media server to fill up a digital, faux Blockbuster.

This is, obviously, not so dissimilar to Boxroom, a game where you can design your own bedroom that lets you use your Steam profile to fill it with games you actually own. With Alt Video, you do things slightly differently just because of the focus on a different format. So, say you have a Letterboxd account. After exporting some data from your account, you can bring that into Alt Video, and this fake video store will then get filled up with shelves of DVD cases of all the films you've watched.

Alternatively, and perhaps more enticingly, if you run something like a Plex or Jellyfin server, you can hook that up to the game too, where again all of the films you own digitally show up in store. What's more interesting here is that there's a cinema room in the store that lets you watch films on your Plex server, and it's possible to invite your Steam friends to watch along with you. There's even a few other rooms, like a '90s bedroom or family room for more of a CRT kinda vibe. It's cute! If you like you can even manually add any DVDs or Blu-rays you own to appear on all the shelves too.

There's a lot of other nice touches too. In the case of your Letterboxd data, your ratings even show up on the back of the boxes. It's not just relegated to films either, you can put in shows or even your games. The whole thing can be played in VR if you really want that immersive feel. There's a store clerk who can give you some recommendations if you're not sure what to watch. And there's even a day and night system, weather, and seasonal shopfront facelifts.

Alt Video is currently slated for release next week on November 24th, and it'll be doing so in early access. Worth noting that for now the focus is on the browsing, but features involving serving customers and running the store are on the way. You can wishlist it on Steam right here.

GTA 6 might only have been with us for a few days, but it's clear from the jump that the level of detail in Rockstar's open world is astonishing. So I asked the GamesRadar+ team to document their favorite little features that might escape your attention if you're not looking very closely. From turn-signals to hyper-efficient snacking techniques, and social media to road condition, here's what impressed us the most in our opening few days.

Barely three hours in, GTA 6's reputation system was something I was still getting my head around, but it was already impressing me. In an early mission where I went to collect rent money for Brian, the store owner got mad at me and pulled a baseball bat. Before he could rush me, I pulled out Jason's pistol and he balked at just the sight of the gun, dropping the bat and agreeing to hand over the payment. I love that the game logged that as an illegal activity, but still one that showed restraint, heightening Jason's reputation as a cool, collected, professional criminal. It's a nuance that few RPGs capture so effectively, and I'm looking forward to how it works over the rest of the game.

They say art imitates life, and that's never been truer than seeing Jason Duval take every opportunity to stuff his face and become a munch goblin in GTA 6. Like when I do it, it's to obtain buffs to my health, stamina, and focus, of course. Choking out police security, I take time to pour myself a mug of java, sipping it as I slink behind cover. After a stressful interaction with a neighbour, I double fist her endless fruit bowl as I crunch apples and leave the cores around her kitchenette. The detail is tremendous – with one hand carrying a crate of beer, Jason will open potato chips one-handed with his mouth before pouring a few bites at a time into his beard-framed mouth. That's my move. I couldn't be prouder.

Jasmine Gould-Wilson, Senior Staff Writer

I have a very particular problem with GTA 6's hyper-realistic car damage mechanics. Specifically, they are so realistic that it makes me panic to even be in my car. The slightest ding against a post box results in an ugly dent in the side of my freshly-painted truck, and don't get me started on how bit of bumper-to-bumper action with another car while squeezing my way onto the highway means an unsightly horizontal scrape all down my… whatever part of the car my door is on. I'm not a cars person, okay? I suck at driving in video games and don't even have my license in the real world (partially because I suck at driving in video games). Yet GTA 6 has me feeling incredibly precious about my ride looking beautiful, and I can't stop visiting every pay and spray in town to address even the tiniest nicks of cosmetic damage.

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

Rockstar has managed to craft a jaw-droppingly realistic world in GTA 6, with gorgeous scenery rich in details that make Leonida feel like a lived-in place. But it's not the graphics that have left me most impressed – it's the devs' attention to detail with the many hilarious Snapmatic shitposts. The in-universe take on Instagram is full of photos and videos from the various residents of Leonida, but the highlights are the ridiculous memes that wouldn't look at all out of place on real-life social media. From "Taco Bomb made me shid my pant" to "do nothing for two hours or straight jork it," an image outside a nursing home captioned "POV: grandma insulted my 6'7 fem-dom goth milk mommy," and Rockstar even parodying the "we got x before GTA 6" memes, I've spent more time scrolling social media in the game over the last day than I have in real life – and, uh, that's saying something. Jason's algorithm is absurd and deeply cursed, and I'm loving it.

I've spent about four hours with GTA 6 so far, and for most of that time, I've been driving. As a bonafide car sicko when it comes to video games, Rockstar's latest is already making my heart go pitter patter. Why? Because I can actually use my car blinkers to indicate when I'm making a turn with the DPad on my PS5 controller. It might sound mundane, but this is a Big Deal to me. It's something I could only dream of when I was cruising around Vice City back in the day, or getting behind the wheel in GTA 5. I've always been one to obey traffic laws in the series, and you better believe I've been stopping at red lights and making way for passing cars. And now I can also indicate each and every turn like a good citizen should? I'm living the dream. What's more, the indicator even automatically switches off when I make my desired turn like a real car. Be still my car-loving heart.

There's a moment in the first chapter where it's time for a party at a local bar, a well-earned celebration in the wake of some good news. Normally this is the sort of thing in a game that'd have me checking my watch and wondering when I can go back to shooting people, but Rockstar's strong writing and character work turn what might've felt like a filler sequence into a moment for developing relationships and story alike (something I can't yet say about the grocery shopping mechanics). But what stuck out for me is just how real it all felt: that one asshole showing up that everybody regrets inviting, the way that people join and split and converge in different groups, the natural rise and fall of energy across the evening. It all ends with a pleasingly solid pool minigame, interrupted by some belligerent drunks who actually snatched my ball off the table as I was about to pot the winning shot, damn it. Alright, now I'm ready to shoot people again.

GTA 6 may be full of thrilling violence and satirical comedy, but my favorite feature so far is its life-sim management elements. Playing as Jason, there's plenty of opportunity to carry out more mundane activities, and the rewards are deeply gratifying. Ahead of Lucia's release from prison, you can repair your home, buy flowers and groceries, and even order a gold necklace to show her how much Jason cares. Lucia's dialogue conveys the character's appreciation, which is nice enough on its own, but the simple act of doing these things also feels good in the moment. Watching Jason roll paint on bare bedroom walls and affix shingles to a leaking roof is soothing, and adds to the sense of immersion because we see the protagonist committing acts of affection that feel real and relatable. I love stealing cars and generally causing mayhem, but I equally enjoy living out more wholesome fantasies in Leonida, and I implore you to do the same.

One of the biggest changes you'll notice in GTA 6 compared to GTA 5 is the ability to choose. Each mission gives you an objective to complete and lets you decide how to do it. Some early-game errands, like rent collection, can get dirty if you really want, though you can also talk people out of making the dumb decision. It's a fresh change that not only takes GTA 6 to the next level but also lets you shape Jason into who you want him to be. I spend my time outside missions being a chill wife guy who fixes up the house and runs errands – so why let a scripted mission run counter to that? My Jason didn't pick that life; it picked him and he's just trying to make it through the best he can.

Obviously there's so much talk about how much of a lived-in world Rockstar Games has created, but one of the ways this has most stuck out to me is through the use of music. Early on I had to head to an artists market to collect some cash from one of Brian's many clientele, but as I parked my car and wandered through the market and heard Elton John's 'I Guess That's Why They Call It The Blues' playing in the distance on a speaker, so instead of immediately walking in to shake down the acid-dealing hippie, I just sort of hung about to listen. I've loved walking into stores to hear a banger playing on their radio, or hanging around areas like that where what song plays gives you a good idea of what the area's culture is like. Perhaps the best use so far has been in the party scene (mentioned above by Joel) where the local band shows up, but instead of just playing licensed music to simulate it, you hear actual covers of classics like Out of Touch by Hall and Oates, to really drive home that local bar feeling.

I've visited Florida quite a bit over the years, but not as a typical tourist. Much of my time there has been spent driving to visit friends who live among the state's smaller towns, and GTA 6 does an incredible job of showcasing just how awful the local roads are. State highways patched over with mismatched blacktop and concrete? Check. Bizarre turn lanes that appear and disappear without a second to get your bearings? Double check. Hastily paved entrances into strip malls that feel like they're going to destroy your car's suspension? Triple check. Leonida has enough similarities to real-life Florida to send a normal driver to a life of crime.

On my Leonida travels, I found a cow that spoke to me. Yes, that sounds insane but I promise it really happened. A runaway pageant cow called Tootsie, dressed in an elaborate red cover, with red bows tied around her ankles, and a fancy flowery hat, made for the hills, leaving me to help the farmer bring her back. I eventually caught up to Tootsie and calmed her down, but then she uttered a chilling "save me". Like Jason, I also physically recoiled at this. I was unsettled for the entire walk back to the farmer, Tootsie now back to regular mooing. Rather than helping the farmer load her into the trailer, I instead shooed Tootsie away, sending her into the sunset. The farmer was - unsurprisingly - livid, saying she wouldn't make it in the wild. I've not seen Tootsie again but I hope she's doing alright.

I'm GamesRadar's Managing Editor for news, shaping the news strategy across the team. I started my journalistic career while getting my degree in English Literature at the University of Warwick, where I also worked as Games Editor on the student newspaper, The Boar. Since then, I've run the news sections at PCGamesN and Kotaku UK, and also regularly contributed to PC Gamer. As you might be able to tell, PC is my platform of choice, so you can regularly find me playing League of Legends or Steam's latest indie hit.

#3660. Ubisoft cuts jobs at major Assassin's Creed and Far Cry studios as its year of layoffs continues

Ubisoft has confirmed more layoffs as part of its previously announced operational "reset", this time affecting 166 employees at its major Montréal and Québec City studios - the teams responsible for game series including Assassin's Creed and Far Cry. It says the cuts are necessary "to ensure our resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs."

GamesIndustry.biz reports the cuts - believed to equate to around four percent of the studios' total headcount - will impact employees working on projects either recently cancelled or significantly changed.

The publication also understands the cuts, said to primarily impact production and support roles at Ubisoft Montréal and Québec City, include members of Vantage Studios - Ubisoft and Tencent's joint development venture announced last October, which focuses on the publisher's biggest franchises, including Far Cry, Rainbow Six Siege, and Assassin's Creed.

In a statement provided to Eurogamer, Ubisoft confirmed it is, "reducing its workforce by 166 positions across its Montréal and Québec City operations", adding: "As our portfolio evolves, our production needs are changing, requiring us to adjust the size of some teams to ensure our resources are aligned with current production priorities and business needs.

"We deeply value the contributions of these teams and recognise the impact this may have on our colleagues," the statement continued. "We are committed to supporting them through this process with care and respect. Those affected are being provided with severance, extended health care benefits, career transition services and other resources."

These latest job cuts are part of a "major organisational, operational and portfolio reset" announced by Ubisoft in January. That initial announcement was accompanied by the news of two studio closures - affecting its Halifax mobile and Stockholm teams - plus the cancellation of six projects, including the much-delayed Prince of Persia: The Sands of Time remake.

Since then, 105 jobs have been cut at Red Storm Entertainment, the Ubisoft studio behind the Ghost Recon series, and around 380 employees were reportedly laid off when the publisher's Winnipeg and Belgrade teams shut in June. In October, Ubisoft closed Trials developer RedLynx and downsized its Singapore Assassin's Creed: Black Flag Resynced team, impacting a total of approximately 120 employees. Amid all this, Ubisoft developers have been on strike in response to the publisher's sweeping layoffs.

While most videogames got out of the way of Grand Theft Auto 6, on the day of its release The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth's free online DLC Repentance+ released an update. It included an easter egg daily challenge called Crime Mode (the seed is V1CE BSMT) with references to GTA like a wanted rating, guns, cops, and cars. Well, driveable minecarts.

What should have been an easy PR win for publisher Nicalis quickly turned sour as players pointed out that the music in Crime Mode sure sounds AI-generated. "It has that 'tinniness' that something like Suno generated music has", user ShweetStuff noted before looking at the music files and finding that, yep, there was Suno metadata in the file comments. Yet there was no AI disclosure on the DLC's Steam page.

Players were not thrilled by this development. Steam user reviews on The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+ dropped to Overwhelmingly Negative, with only 8% positive recent reviews. Players put the blame on Nicalis, who licence Binding of Isaac from its original creator Edmund McMillen. "Edmund please take back control of the game", one said.

"Woke up to a shit show," McMillen wrote on the hatesite formerly known as Twitter when he found out what had happened, "obviously I had no idea it featured generated music in the daily run, looking into how that happened and getting it removed, stay tuned."

As of the latest update, the AI-generated music is gone. "It's a little sad given Joey Kuras (game's sound designer) did some excellent sounds for Mewgenics", ShweetStuff wrote, "but I suppose this is the industry nowadays!"

#3658. The Sunday Papers

The Sunday Papers is our weekly roundup of great writing about (mostly) videogames from across the web.

Sundays are for googling local purveyors of live Christmas trees, the sole upside of no longer having a cat being that you can once again enjoy the smell of chopped woodland without the risk of it poisoning a family member. Well, then again, I mean... empirically speaking, you're probably just assuming that your human loved ones haven't eaten spruce needles. Can you say for an absolute fact that they wouldn't?

Fortunately, while your nan is off having her stomach pumped, you can pass the time by reading some good words from this week.

First up is, if I'm honest, nepotism. But there's also no rule against the Sunday Papers including RPS staff when they're not writing for RPS, so in the interests of spreading understanding about games media's most underappreciated discipline, here's our own guides writer Jeremy Blum on the making of his (excellent) Castlevania: Belmont's Curse walkthrough.

Ah, sod it, here's more Inside Baseball, as Reuters' Matthew Leake looks out at the shining sea to behold the creaking, precarious flotsam-raft we call games journalism. Fun fact: prior to editing, this quoted our good friend and former colleague, Brian Caldwell.

I continue to eagerly read about Marathon, I game I have zero intention of playing myself. This time it's Artemis Octavio for Skybox, on inhabiting the metal skin of the Rook.

Over on Unwinnable, Justin Reeve considers the distinctly American flavour of violence running through the Red Dead Redemption series.

Professor and author Dave Karpf checks in on the tech CEO class, who are definitely having a normal one now that a comrade is under the microscope.

Finally, five words: Neil the Seal Management Plan.

Music this week is, oh I don't know, let's say Beach Bunny. See you tomorrow.
